Category: Abstract.
Subject: wind-walking beach creature of tubes.
Style: Theo Jansen kinetic sculpture.

spec.name: Strandbeest Windwalker
spec.description: A Theo Jansen-style kinetic beach creature: yellow PVC-tube lattice body on two crankshafts, eight Jansen-linkage legs, bottle-and-cloth wind wings, a bottle-eyed head with a split jaw and a windvane tail.
spec.layout: Long, low insect-like walker facing +Z. Everything is thin yellow PVC tubes (radius 0.02 to 0.035) joined at black ball joints and wrapped with black zip ties and blue tape rings, with translucent blue bottles and white sail cloth as the only broad surfaces. Bottom to top: eight sand-padded feet on y=0, eight identical Jansen linkage legs hanging from the frame, with 4 leg planes at x=+0.5, +1.0, -0.5, -1.0 on each of two crankshafts (front axle z=+1.0, rear axle z=-1.0, both at y=1.2). Above them the lattice frame (two lower rails at x=+-0.25, y=1.45, one spine at y=1.95, zig-zag W trusses between them) runs z=-1.8..1.7. Two big bottle-sail wings rise from the spine with a dihedral (root x=+-0.45,y=1.95; tip x=+-1.3,y=2.25), chord z=-1.4..1.4. A bank of blue pressure bottles hangs under the middle of the frame between the axles. A tube head with a bottle muzzle, separate upper and lower jaw, and two bottle eyes sits at the front. A three-segment windvane tail trails at the back. The Jansen look shows everywhere: no smooth skin, only rods, balls, ties, tape and bottles; every node has a black ball joint. All units in the leg spec below are meters, scaled so the rest pose is a standing walker with all feet on the floor.

parts.builds: The structural lattice and drive, all in pvcYellow tubes (radius 0.03 main, 0.02 braces) with jointBlack ball/elbow connectors (sphere r 0.045) at every node, zipBlack ties, tapeBlue tape rings and pvcYellowDark end plugs. (1) Two lower rails at x=+-0.25, y=1.45, from z=-1.7 to z=1.7. (2) One spine tube at x=0, y=1.95, from z=-1.5 to z=1.5 (ends flare down via braces). (3) Zig-zag W lattice: slanted braces from each rail up to the spine, one every 0.3 m in z, alternating lean (about 24 braces), plus horizontal cross-ties at x=0..+-0.25 every 0.6 m. (4) Front and rear converging truss: rods from rail ends (+-0.25,1.45,+-1.7) and spine ends up/down to the mounts headBase [0,1.65,1.75] and tailBase [0,1.65,-1.75] (frame rods END at those mounts; head/tail parts start there). (5) Two crankshafts along x at y=1.2, z=+1.0 (joint crankF) and z=-1.0 (joint crankR), each a steel tube radius 0.025 from x=-1.22 to x=1.22, with brass end knobs, jointBlack bearing blocks at x=+-0.25 and posts (radius 0.02) rising from each bearing to the rails at y=1.45. (6) Two pivot axles along x at y=1.28, z=0.62 (pivotF) and z=-1.38 (pivotR), pvcYellow tubes radius 0.02 from x=-1.12 to x=1.12 with posts to the rails, and tape rings where each leg plane (x=+-0.5, +-1.0) meets them. (7) A drive chain loop in the plane x=0 between two toothed sprockets (lathe discs, steel, radius 0.1, at the crank axle centres) made of small zipBlack link boxes along two straight runs. (8) Two flat sail-mast stubs where the wings mount: short yellow tubes from the spine at (+-0.45,1.95,0) pointing up and outwards, topped with jointBlack hinge blocks (the wing parts start at the wingRoot mounts). Trim: accentRed tape ring on the crankshaft centre, zip ties in pairs on every lattice node.
parts.attaches: Crankshaft centres at mounts crankF/crankR (legs builders draw their crank arms from these points). Pivot axles at pivotF/pivotR (legs hang from them). Truss ends at headBase and tailBase. Wing roots at wingRootL/R.

parts.builds: Four identical Jansen linkage legs on the FRONT crankshaft (axle centre C = crankF = [x, 1.2, 1.0]): one at each plane x = +0.5, +1.0, -0.5, -1.0. Use this exact planar linkage in leg-local coordinates (u = world z offset from the axle, v = world y offset from y=1.2, x = plane x): C(0,0) crank axle; Cp(0.10,-0.11) crank pin; P(-0.38,0.08) fixed pivot (sits on pivotF axle at world [x,1.28,0.62]); A(-0.35,-0.33); D(-0.62,-0.17); K(-0.52,-0.60); E(0.18,-0.62); F(-0.14,-0.91); T(0.12,-1.12) ankle/foot centre (world y 0.08). World point = [x, 1.2+v, 1.0+u]. Rods (pvcYellow, radius 0.018, flat caps): crank arm C-Cp (brass, radius 0.022, laid on the outer layer), P-A, Cp-A, P-D, A-D, D-K, A-K, Cp-E, A-E, shank K-T (passes through F, pvcYellowLight, radius 0.022), E-F, E-T. Layering: rods of the crank arm, Cp-A, Cp-E and E-F/E-T sit on the outer layer (x offset +0.04 away from the mid-plane, so for negative x planes offset toward -x); all other rods sit on the plane x. Every node gets a jointBlack ball (r 0.032; r 0.04 at P, Cp and K), brass crank pin, a steel crank hub disc (cylinder r 0.06 along x) at C, and zipBlack ties (small boxes) at the nodes. Foot: sandPad sphere r 0.08 centred on T with a flatter sandDark disc cap under it, a capOrange bottle-cap ring above and a short tapeBlue wrap on the shank above it. Bones: hipXX0/1 own the P-A, P-D, A-D, D-K, A-K, upper rods; shankXX0/1 own the shank K-T below F, E-F, E-T and the foot (names hipFL0 shankFL0 hipFL1 shankFL1 hipFR0 shankFR0 hipFR1 shankFR1). Feet bottoms on y=0.
parts.attaches: Hangs on the pivotF axle (frame) at P and wraps the crankF shaft at C (hub sits on the shaft).

parts.builds: Identical copy of the front legs, on the REAR crankshaft (C = crankR = [x, 1.2, -1.0]), same four planes x = +0.5, +1.0, -0.5, -1.0, same direction of travel (+Z). Exact planar linkage in leg-local coordinates (u = world z offset from the axle, v = world y offset from y=1.2, x = plane x): C(0,0) crank axle; Cp(0.10,-0.11) crank pin; P(-0.38,0.08) fixed pivot (world [x,1.28,-1.38] on pivotR); A(-0.35,-0.33); D(-0.62,-0.17); K(-0.52,-0.60); E(0.18,-0.62); F(-0.14,-0.91); T(0.12,-1.12) (world y 0.08). World point = [x, 1.2+v, -1.0+u]. Rods (pvcYellow, radius 0.018, flat caps): crank arm C-Cp (brass, r 0.022, outer layer), P-A, Cp-A, P-D, A-D, D-K, A-K, Cp-E, A-E, shank K-T through F (pvcYellowLight, r 0.022), E-F, E-T. Outer layer (offset 0.04 away from the mid-plane in x): crank arm, Cp-A, Cp-E, E-F, E-T; the rest on the plane. jointBlack balls (r 0.032; 0.04 at P, Cp, K) at every node, brass crank pin, steel hub disc (r 0.06 along x) at C, zipBlack ties at nodes. Foot: sandPad sphere r 0.08 at T, sandDark flat disc below, capBlue ring cap above (blue instead of orange, to read as the rear set), tapeBlue wrap on the shank. Bones: hip/shank joints named hipRL0 shankRL0 hipRL1 shankRL1 hipRR0 shankRR0 hipRR1 shankRR1 with the same ownership split as the front legs (upper rods on hip, shank/E-F/E-T/foot on shank). Feet bottoms on y=0.
parts.attaches: Hangs on the pivotR axle (frame) at P and wraps the crankR shaft at C.

parts.builds: Two mirrored bottle-sail wings (left joint sailL / sailTipL at +x, right sailR / sailTipR at -x), each rising from its wingRoot mount (+-0.45,1.95,0) to its wingTip mount (+-1.3,2.25,0): a dihedral of about 19 degrees. Each wing: a root spar and a tip spar (pvcYellow tubes radius 0.025) running along z from -1.4 to +1.4, a leading and trailing edge tube joining them at z=+-1.4, jointBlack corner balls, and a centre rib. Between the spars a row of 14 translucent bottleBlue bottles (lathe or tapered cylinder, radius 0.085, length 0.8 along the span direction, 8 segments, with a bottleBlueDeep shoulder ring and a cap alternating capBlue and capOrange at the outer end) are strapped side by side along z, with sailWhite cloth triangles (thin extrudes, sailShade on their lower faces) stretched between bottle pairs on the trailing side, rope (rope colour) lashing bands and zipBlack ties around every bottle at the spars, and an accentRed pennant on each tip. The inner half of each wing rides sailL / sailR, the outer half rides sailTipL / sailTipR. Keep the top at y<=2.3 and the width at x=+-1.3.
parts.attaches: Wing roots hinge on the mast stub blocks at wingRootL/R (built by the frame).

parts.builds: Three self-contained pieces on the body line. (1) HEAD starting at mount headBase [0,1.65,1.75], joint head, extending to z=2.2: a yellow tube skull frame (a diamond of rods radius 0.025, jointBlack balls) with a bottleBlue bottle as the muzzle forming a rigid upper jaw (cap capOrange at the tip, rope bands) and a separate lower jaw of two yellow tubes plus a smaller bottle on joint jaw (hinge at [0,1.6,1.95]); two big bottle eyes on the sides at x=+-0.13: eyeWhite spheres r 0.07 with pupil discs and a tapeBlue ring, capOrange brow caps above; two long thin feeler rods (pvcYellowLight, r 0.012) swept up and forward from the brow with jointBlack ball tips; an accentRed tape band across the skull. (2) TAIL starting at tailBase [0,1.65,-1.75], joints tail1 tail2 tail3, three tapering yellow tubes (radius 0.03 to 0.015) running back to z=-2.2 with jointBlack knuckles and zipBlack ties, ending in a small sailWhite triangular windvane (extrude) with an accentRed edge. (3) BELLY BANK centred at bellyBankCenter [0,1.25,0] on joint body: 2 rows x 4 bottleBlue pressure bottles lying along z (radius 0.07, length 0.28, capBlue caps at the rear, 8 segments) at x=+-0.14, y=1.25 and y=1.25 stacked rows at z=-0.55..0.55, strapped with rope bands and a hose of thin zipBlack tube linking the caps to a small steel pump cylinder, hung from the rails (ties up to railL/railR at y=1.45). Keep the bank clear of the legs (|x|<0.3 only).
parts.attaches: Head and tail start exactly at headBase / tailBase where the frame truss ends; the belly bank hangs from the lower rails at railL/railR.

calls.reasoning:
I'm envisioning a Strandbeest-style wind-walking creature built from yellow PVC tubes, white sail wings, and zip ties, using Jansen linkage legs on a shared crankshaft, and sketching out rough dimensions of about 2.6 wide, 2.4 tall, and 4.0 long.

Now I'm working out the mechanical layout: a crankshaft running along the X-axis with planar leg linkages stacked in parallel YZ-plane modules on either side, while the creature's body and sails extend along Z as the walking direction.

Rather than mirroring legs left/right separately, I'll have each builder construct both sides via a symmetric loop over outer and inner leg planes, using the same Jansen linkage proportions (a=38.0, b=41.5, c=39.3, d=40.1) so the geometry stays consistent even though the code itself can't be shared.

I'm scaling the linkage so the leg stands roughly 1.1m tall with the foot dropping about 0.9m below the pivot, and I'm placing the crank's fixed pivot point relative to the frame so the crank radius (0.15m) and crank center offset (a, l) match Jansen's original numbers. I'm now working out an approximate rest-pose angle for the crank so I can derive starting joint coordinates in the z-forward, y-up frame.

I'm working out placeholder coordinates for the crank pin and frame pivot relative to the axle center, picking rough values like Cp at (-0.13, -0.075) and P somewhere around (0.38, -0.08), since the exact position doesn't matter for this static layout, just that the rods connect sensibly.

Still computing coordinates... I'm placing the crank axle at the origin, finding the pin position with a 0.15 radius, then working out point A by triangulating from P and Cp using the known rod lengths 0.415 and 0.5.

The exact Jansen linkage closure math is getting unwieldy, so I decide to abandon trying to match the precise geometry and instead sketch my own visually plausible leg shape with approximate coordinates for the knee triangle and foot point, prioritizing a convincing silhouette over exact linkage physics.

Still working out the leg linkage coordinates...

I need to figure out the world height so the foot sits near the floor, which sets the crank's resting height. Jansen's actual mechanism staggers the leg phases across the eight planes for a smooth walking gait, but that complicates a shared spec, so I'm leaning toward keeping all planes synchronized with the same phase for simplicity, maybe just alternating left/right by 180°.

I'm also working out where the frame and axle sit in world coordinates relative to the legs, plus stacking up the total height — legs around 1.2, frame above that, and sails on top — to land on an overall figure near 2.2.

Now I'm thinking through how to arrange crankshaft groups and leg spacing along the length so the geometry stays within a reasonable plane budget, weighing a couple layout options for how many planes per side before settling on something that fits the total count.

For sails I'll go with Jansen-style wing sails made of rows of translucent pale blue bottle-lathe cylinders on mast stalks with cross yards, topped with white cloth panels, plus a front bowsprit cluster of feeler tubes with sand-anchor bottles.

Now I'm planning the head and ballast section: a front prow with a proboscis, orange tube eyes, and pressure bottles along the belly that store wind like Jansen's Animaris Ordis. Then I'm laying out the five main parts, starting with the frame — spine truss, crankshafts, drive chain, cross braces, pivot mounts, and the pivot axle tubes positioned along the frame's x-axis at a fixed height.

Working out the frame geometry now, placing the longitudinal rails and legs' pivot points, and positioning the lower rails and upper spine with triangular support struts.

I'm also figuring out the leg plane arrangement for the front and rear axles, checking that four planes per axle at x=±0.5 and ±1.0 properly clear the crankshaft without collision.

For rigging, I'm planning the joint hierarchy: a root spine joint for the body, hinge joints at each crank axle, and figuring out how to handle the legs since a parallelogram linkage doesn't map cleanly onto a simple tree chain—leaning toward giving each leg plane its own joint reference.

For the legs, I'll set up hip-to-shank chains per plane (hipFL0, shankFL0, etc.) tagged with a "leg" role, giving 16 joints across 8 legs, plus the crank, body, head, and jaw joints for the separate upper and lower mandible.

I'm adding a jaw structure to the head for a creature touch, giving it a split beak made of two tube bottles, plus sail masts tagged as wing-role joints and a trailing windvane-style tail chain. Now I'm starting to tally up the final part list, beginning with the frame assembly containing the spine truss, crankshafts, pivots, and drive chain.

Breaking out remaining parts: front and rear leg assemblies, a sails group with wing joints, and a combined head/tail section with jaws, bottle eyes, feeler tubes, a three-segment windvane tail, and a ballast bank of pressure bottles -- all fitting within a 900-part budget split across frame, legs, sails, and head/tail. I'm then laying out the body length along the z-axis, positioning the head toward the front, tail toward the rear, and sizing the frame rails to fit between them.

Now I'm working out the crank axle positions at the front and rear, mapping each leg's local coordinates into world space, and checking that the front and rear leg swing ranges along z don't overlap or collide with each other. I'm also figuring out how to offset the crank arms and link rods slightly to each side of the central plane so the layered leg components don't intersect.

Now I'm calculating the foot positions and ball radii so the feet rest just at floor level without clipping through, and sketching out the overall frame height so the mast base, spine top, and sail tips line up to the target total height of 2.3.

For the sails, I'm planning two mast assemblies mounted symmetrically (one at +x, one at -x) rising to about 2.25, each carrying crossing yards along z with rows of small bottle shapes to simulate sail cloth, framed as trapezoidal wing-sail panels spanning the upper y-range.

I'm also sketching out the coordinate mounts for the crank and pivot points that anchor these mast structures to the main body.

Working out bounding boxes for each component now: the frame spans roughly x ±1.25 with crankshaft ends at ±1.22, the legs box extends front and rear with the pivot sitting around y 1.3, and the sails box covers x ±1.3, y 1.9-2.3, z ±1.5.

Now I'm defining the head/tail box combining into one span from roughly [-0.55, 1.1, -2.2] to [0.55, 2.0, 2.2], accepting some overlap with other parts, while also placing the belly bottles between the crankshaft groups around x ±0.15 at y 1.1-1.35.

I'm checking the belly bank placement sits clear of the legs, then working out the color palette: yellows for the PVC tubing, blacks for joints and zip ties, whites and tints for the sail, and blues for the bottles with their caps.

Now I'm laying out the joint hierarchy—spine root, front and rear crank positions, and the per-leg hip joints indexed by axle and side.

Working out the hip and shank joint direction vectors more carefully, I'll set the rear leg hips and shanks at z=-1.38 and z=-1.14 respectively. Then I'm defining the sail joints on either side of the body with outward-angled tip directions, giving them a wing role.

Now I'm placing the head and jaw joints along with the three tail segments, assigning hinge positions and directions for each so the chain extends naturally outward and downward.

I'm organizing the skeleton into named groups—frame, legsFront, legsRear, sails, head—and sketching the head's construction: a tube-frame skull with a bottle-based muzzle, upper and lower jaw tubes, bottle-cap eyes with painted pupils, and thin forward-pointing feeler tubes with ball tips, all bounded within a compact head region.

For the tail I'm tapering three tube segments down to a small sail-vane triangle secured with zip ties, and underneath the body I'm placing a bladder bank of blue bottles arranged in two rows along the central axis, strapped to the frame with rope bands near the crank axles. I'm also setting rough part budgets (frame, front/rear legs, sails, head/tail) that sum to the total, and noting I still need to spell out the leg linkage mechanism.

Now I'm plotting out the exact linkage geometry for the leg mechanism, defining coordinate points for the crank, pivots, and connecting rods (crank arm, upper and lower links, shank, and foot) relative to the crank axle, along with how they connect into a chain down to a foot ball with a flat sand-contact disc at the bottom.

I'm adding small ball-joint spheres and zip-tie fasteners at each node, then layering rods across two x-offset planes so they don't collide -- the crank arm and its adjacent links sit on an outer plane while the rest stay flush. I'm also working out how the top pivot and crank axle connect back to frame-built shafts and hubs, since the legs piece only builds the arm and disc while the frame supplies the actual axle.

Tallying per-plane part counts (rods, balls, feet, hubs, ties, pins) to check I'm staying within budget, then moving on to the frame itself -- crankshaft tubes with brass knobs, pivot tubes, lower rails, an upper spine, and a zigzag lattice of struts connecting them Jansen-style.

Now I'm detailing the drive mechanism: a chain or belt loop linking the crank axles via small sprocket discs, plus connector elbows, tube end plugs, and tape wraps, and working out the vertical support posts that tie the pivot axles and crankshaft bearings into the rails.

I'm also mapping out the head and tail mounts, having the front and rear rails converge toward headBase and tailBase points, with the spine frame sloping down to meet the head attachment. Now I'm starting on the wing structure, anchoring the wing root at the mast position.

Still planning wing geometry... the wing is a wide inclined plane with a long chord running along z, leading and trailing tubes from root to tip, spars, and ribs, with bottles arranged radially along the span to fill out the blade shape.

I'm budgeting about 80 bottles per wing in a louver-like row with caps and connecting rope, maybe two rows offset, plus a top yard and leave cloth paneling details to the builder, with joints splitting each wing into inner and outer sections. I still need to make sure the overall bounding box matches the sail dimensions.

Let me finalize the sail box dimensions and confirm the wing height clears properly, then lock in the Jansen-style material palette (yellow PVC tubes, black zip ties, blue tape, translucent bottles, sandy tones) along with rod radius conventions for the frame, legs, and crankshaft before writing out the final JSON spec.

I'm setting up a coordinate helper to map leg-local positions into world space, then defining key joint points for the rear leg structure.

Cross-checking these points against the joint spec, I confirm hip, shank, and foot positions line up correctly, with the K-F-T segment roughly collinear so I can split it into two connected rod pieces without visual breaks. I'm also working out the sand contact detail — a thin disc cap sitting just under the foot sphere where it touches the ground, making sure nothing dips below floor level.

Now I need to decide bone assignment for each rod: most of the upper linkage (P-A, Cp-A, P-D, A-D, D-K, A-K, Cp-E, A-E, K-F, crank arm) attaches to the hip bone, while the shank bone carries F-T, E-F, E-T, and the foot, with the shared joint E's ball placed on the shank side.

For the outer-layer offset, I'm offsetting rod endpoints along x by a small amount depending on sign, and at shared nodes like Cp, A, E, and F I'm adding a short connecting pin between the inner-plane ball and a smaller outer-layer ball so the two layers stay linked mechanically.

I'm positioning the hub disc at the crankshaft center so the crank arm sits flush against it, then modeling the crank pin as a brass rod extending from the plane outward to Cp with a ball cap at the end.

Still placing joint balls at each node, then adding the foot sphere at T with a tape-wrap cylinder along the shank direction and a cap ring positioned just above the foot sphere.

Now I'm figuring out zip ties: thin ring-shaped cylinders wrapped around the rods near each node, placed a short distance along the rod direction with a dark color to simulate real zip ties.

Counting parts per leg quickly, I realize the naive total (rods, balls, pins, hub, foot components, ties) balloons to roughly 45 per leg, which across 8 legs blows well past the 200-part budget. So I need to merge geometries sharing the same bone and color into single combined meshes to cut the part count down to something like 24 per leg instead.

Reworking the budget with merging by color group per leg gets me to around 12 parts per leg, which times 8 legs lands safely under 200. Since the built-in rod-creation helper generates its own separate mesh per sweep, I'll instead construct my own cylinder geometries directly—building a cylinder between two points by orienting it with a quaternion from the default axis to the desired direction and translating it to the midpoint—so these can be merged alongside the other geometry groups.

I'll use the SDK's aim helper to compute that orientation quaternion directly, then build each cylinder with low-poly segments (7-8 sides) and flat shading for a faceted look, applying the quaternion and position offset before merging. I'm setting up a collector that bins geometry by bone and color, then at the end flushes each bin into a single merged part call with flat shading enabled.

Now I'm estimating triangle budgets — with 8-sided cylinders and spheres per leg, the total across 8 legs blows past the 12000 triangle budget, so I need to cut costs by making ties simple boxes instead of cylinders, dropping rod sides to 6, and using lower-resolution spheres for the balls to bring the total back down.

Still defining tie placements...

Now I'm setting up the leg mirroring scheme across the four x-positions, naming joints like hipRL0 with side signs determining outward offsets, and building out the bone hierarchy for each leg.

Working out the hub disc and crank arm geometry, positioning the steel cylinder along the x-axis and checking that the brass arm's radius fits within the hub thickness.

I decide to keep the hub rigidly attached to the hip bone since it rides the crankshaft, and add a small brass bolt detail merged into that part. Now I'm assigning joint-black balls to the various node positions, mapping which ones belong to the hip versus the shank bones.

Then I work through which rods sit on the outer layer versus the central plane: the crank arm and connections from Cp, E, F, T sit outer, while most other rods like P-A, P-D, A-D, D-K, A-K lie on the plane, with A-E being an exception that also sits on the plane. I'm figuring out where pins need to bridge between outer and plane layers at connection nodes like A, E, and F, and considering how the crank pin passes through at Cp where nothing sits on the plane.

Now I'm sizing the components: the crank pin extends outward from the plane with radius 0.075s, outer balls at Cp use radius 0.04, while A, E, F each need an outer ball (0.028), a plane ball (0.032), and a connecting pin (0.012) which I'll treat as steel-colored even if conceptually brass. I'm tallying up how many pins and balls are needed at each joint, and setting the foot as a sphere with radius 0.08.

Adding shank components...

I'm defining tie placements along each rod as fractional points between endpoints, then building a rod table with keys for position, radius, color, and bone association so ties can reference them. I'm keeping the tie geometry simple, just collar wraps without extra tail details, and setting rod cylinders to a small radius with hexagonal cross-sections.

For the function signature, I'm destructuring the context object with the builder, joints, parts, and materials, then indexing joint names dynamically per side and index. I'm merging all the cylinder, sphere, and box geometries using BufferGeometryUtils after applying rotations and translations, keeping them faceted rather than smooth-shaded to match the flat styling.

Now I'm sketching helper functions: one to build a rod geometry between two points by computing direction, length, and orientation via a quaternion, then translating it to the midpoint, and another to handle bone naming and flush logic keyed by bone name and color. I'm working through the leg loop and tie geometry, orienting boxes along the rod direction at each joint point, then moving on to the pivot ball radius.

Defining more rods...

I'm drafting the buildLegsFront function signature using the provided Ctx type, following the existing template pattern for consistency with the joint structure.

Now I'm working out the geometry: mapping hip, shank, and foot positions for each leg (FL0, FL1, FR0, FR1), creating a helper for plane points, and deciding how rods attach to bones with explicit bone references. I'm placing ball joints at each structural node and figuring out how the outer and mid-layer rods offset to connect properly.

I'm worried about hitting the 200-part budget, so I'm counting rods, balls, pins, and ties per leg and realizing it adds up too fast across four legs. To cut the count, I'm planning to merge the tie boxes per bone into single parts using geometry merging, and considering doing the same for balls.

Adding rod and cylinder helpers...

Working out the tie box rotation about the x-axis so its thin edge aligns with the rod's direction in the z-y plane, matching the angle θ to the rod vector components.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton points for the mechanism in (u,v) coordinates—crank center, pin, pivots, and linkage joints—and starting to assign each rod segment to its owner bone and material, like the brass crank arm connecting C to Cp.

Checking whether F lies exactly on the K-T shank line confirms it does at t≈0.594, so the shank K-T is split into two sub-segments at F, with the K-F portion belonging to the hip assembly and F-T continuing as the shank's own piece.

I'm now assigning ball joint radii and parent rods to each vertex — P, Cp, K get hip ownership, while E sits at the junction between hip rods (Cp-E, A-E) and shank rods (E-F, E-T), so I'll just assign it to hip since the geometry works out identically either way.

Now I'm working out the hub disc dimensions for the crank mechanism — placing the steel hub cylinder along the shaft axis, sizing the brass crank pin cylinder at Cp, and positioning the hub so it properly covers the crank arm's connection points without clipping the shaft.

I'm adding small outer-layer balls at Cp, E, and A to cap the rod ends, checking that they overlap enough with the connecting rods to look seamless, then adding thin steel connector pins running along x at each joint to tie the parts together.

Still shaping the foot geometry...

Writing orientation helper...

Now I'm working out tie placements at the rod nodes, using black zip-tie color, placing them near rod ends with offsets scaled to rod length to keep triangle counts manageable across all four legs.

Defining the four hip joints by side and index, naming them like hipFL0, and considering whether to add a small pivot sleeve at each joint point using a dark yellow cylinder segment.

I'm double-checking the leg's bounding box against the frame limits—verifying hub, pin, and foot positions stay within the ±1.1 x-range and the 0.3–1.3 z-range. Now I'm writing a merge helper function that groups geometry by bone and color into a map for combining meshes efficiently.

Continuing the merge logic, I'm confirming that mixed geometry types like spheres, cylinders, boxes, and torus shapes can all be combined since they share position, normal, and UV attributes, then setting up a cylinder-along-x helper that rotates and translates a standard cylinder geometry into place.

Now I'm working out the tie helper for connecting two world points — computing the direction vector and angle so a small box geometry rotates correctly to bridge the gap, wrapping around the rod with a slightly wider box than the rod's radius to avoid gaps.

Defining more rod data...

I'm planning the buildHeadTail function, using the provided Ctx type and setting up joint positions like head and jaw with their coordinates and directions.
